inline.s: Sentient beings each have their own Way; let each cultivate and not hinder or trouble the other. To leave the Way of one’s own mind and seek the Way outside—to the very end of life, one will not see the Way.

The Essentials of Mind Transmission says: “Only this one mind—there is not so much as a particle of Dharma to be obtained; this very mind is Buddha. Now those who study the Way, not awakening to the essence of this mind, generate a mind upon the mind and seek Buddha outside; practicing while clinging to marks—all these are unwholesome Dharmas, not the Way of bodhi.” “Only this one mind is Buddha; Buddha and sentient beings are in no way different. It is only that sentient beings, clinging to marks, seek outside, and the more they seek the more they lose—making the Buddha seek the Buddha, using the mind to catch the mind, through kalpas without number and throughout life never obtaining it. They do not know that by stilling thoughts and forgetting considerations, the Buddha appears before them of itself.”

[Beings possessed of color] Sentient beings who have a body of form. [Seeing the Way] Seeing the Way, cultivating the Way, and the Way of no-more-learning are together called the three Ways. In the Mahayana, the first stage (bhumi) is called seeing the Way; the second through the ninth stages are called cultivating the Way; and the tenth stage up to Buddhahood is called the Way of no-more-learning. To see one’s original nature completely is the first stage, and is called seeing the Way.

[Drifting to and fro for a whole lifetime, at the end still wearying oneself. If you would see the true Way, conduct that is upright is itself the Way. If you yourself have no mind for the Way, walking in darkness you will not see the Way.]

One who does not polish and realize one’s own mind upon the states and conditions, but thinks the Way is elsewhere, rushes about in all directions for a lifetime searching, and at the end still is vexed that he has not seen the Way; if you would see the true Way, conduct that is upright (not clinging) is itself the Way. If you yourself have no mind for the Way, it is like walking a road at night—you cannot see the Way.
[Drifting to and fro (bo-bo)] Rushing about.
This passage says that the Way lies right in one’s own present place, not to be turned by the states and conditions; conduct that is upright (not clinging) is itself the Way.

[One who truly cultivates the Way does not see the faults of the world. If one sees the wrongs of others, one’s own fault is then the wrong. Another’s wrong I do not make my wrong; if I make a wrong, that is my own fault.]

If one is a true cultivator of the Way, one will not see the faults of the world. If one sees that others are wrong and censures them in one’s own mind, then one has oneself erred. Another’s wrong—I must not take it as wrong; if I take it as wrong (censuring others in my own mind), then I myself have a fault.

Removing the discriminating mind is most crucial for cultivating the Way. So the Sixth Patriarch, in “Chapter Eight, Sudden and Gradual,” instructs: “The ground of mind without wrong—this is the precept of self-nature.” (When the ground of mind does not give rise to right and wrong, self and other, that is the precept of self-nature.)
[Only put aside the mind that censures—strike and break through afflictions. With love and hate unheeded in the mind, stretch out both feet and lie down.]

As long as one puts away the mind that censures others, one will break through many afflictions; when the feelings of love and hate no longer rise in the mind, then at all times and in all places one is at ease and free.

[With love and hate unheeded in the mind, stretch out both feet and lie down] The mind being empty, the realms are empty of themselves; the myriad dharmas bind nothing, and one is fundamentally liberated.
[If you would transform others, you yourself must have the skillful means. Do not let them have doubt—this is the manifestation of self-nature.]
If you would use the Sudden Teaching to transform others, you yourself must have the skillfully appropriate means; to not cause them to have doubt—this is the manifestation of self-nature.
[The Buddha-Dharma is in the world, and is not separate from the world’s awakening. To seek bodhi apart from the world is like seeking the horn of a rabbit.]

The Buddha-Dharma is in the world; to awaken, one cannot be apart from the world. To seek bodhi apart from the world is exactly like seeking the horn of a rabbit, which does not exist at all—for there is no awakening apart from the world!

[Not separate from the world’s awakening] The Platform Sutra especially emphasizes testing the mind amid the states of affairs. One must examine and temper oneself upon the states of affairs; these states of affairs are the tongs and the hammer. Apart from the tempering of the states of affairs, one cannot cut off afflictions and escape the three realms—much less realize the Way and become Buddha!

“The world” refers to the three realms: the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the realm of formlessness. The Buddha-Dharma is the teaching that leaves the false and realizes the true; it is a transcendent Dharma. This is the watershed between the Buddha-Dharma and the way of Confucius and Mencius, the externalist schools, and the externalists attached to Buddhism. Yet the Buddha-Dharma exists within the world, and one must in the world test the mind amid the states of affairs, so as to break clinging and remove habits—to subdue afflictions and cut off afflictions, and so transcend the world. (The Pure Land method, by only subduing afflictions and reciting the Buddha’s name with the aim of rebirth in the Western Paradise of Ultimate Bliss, suffices to end birth and death and escape the three realms; other methods must cut off afflictions in order to end birth and death and escape the three realms.)

This says that one must work at the very place of meeting affairs and objects, rather than fleeing from the states of affairs. A cultivator who leaves the grinding and polishing of the world is like the flowers and plants of a hothouse, unable to withstand wind and rain—how could he realize the Way and become Buddha?

[The tempering of the states of affairs] Tempering is the ancient method by which raw iron is turned into steel—the so-called “a hundred refiner’s hammerings make steel.” The method is: raw iron, by repeated high-temperature hammering, is freed of its impurities and reduced in its carbon content, and so becomes steel. “The tempering of the states of affairs” is the grinding and polishing upon the states of affairs by which one removes affliction and ignorance. [Externalists attached to Buddhism] Sects that, by latching onto Buddhism, distort and tamper with its doctrines.
[Right view is called transcending the world; wrong view is called the world. When both wrong and right are struck down, the nature of bodhi stands revealed.]
Right view is called transcending the world, and wrong view is called the world; when both wrong view and right view are struck down, the bodhi-nature stands clearly revealed.
[This verse is the Sudden Teaching, and is also called the great Dharma-boat. The confused, hearing it, pass through many kalpas; the awakened, then, is in an instant.]

This Verse of No-Marks is the Sudden-Teaching mind-Dharma, and is the great Dharma-boat that conveys beings to the other shore of nirvana; the confused, hearing it, do not awaken through many kalpas, while sudden awakening is in but a moment.

[The Master again said: Today, in the Great Brahma Temple, having spoken this Sudden Teaching, I pray that all sentient beings in the Dharma-realm may, upon these words, see nature and become Buddha. At that time Prefect Wei, together with the officials and the religious and lay followers, hearing what the Master taught, all without exception came to awareness. They all at once made obeisance, and all exclaimed: Well done! Whoever would have thought that in Lingnan a Buddha had appeared in the world.]

The Master again said: Today, in the Great Brahma Temple, I have spoken this Sudden Teaching, and pray that all sentient beings in the Dharma-realm may, at this very moment, see nature and become Buddha. At that time Prefect Wei, together with the officials and the religious (those gone forth) and the lay (those at home), hearing the Master’s instruction, all without exception came to awareness, and together made obeisance to the Master. All praised it, saying: How well spoken! We never thought that in Lingnan a Buddha had appeared in the world.

[One day, Prefect Wei prepared for the Master a great assembly-feast. When the feast was finished, the Prefect asked the Master to ascend the seat, and together with the officials, scholars, and commoners, with solemn mien, made obeisance again, asking: Your disciple, having heard the Reverend speak the Dharma, finds it truly inconceivable. Now I have a small doubt, and beg the Teacher, in great compassion, to explain it for me. The Master said: If you have a doubt, ask, and I shall speak it for you.]

One day, Prefect Wei set up for the Master a great unrestrained assembly. When the feast was done, the Prefect invited the Master to ascend the Dharma-seat, and together with the officials and the gathered community, with solemn mien, made obeisance again, asking: The disciple, having heard the Reverend speak the Dharma, finds it profound, subtle, and penetrating—truly inconceivable. The disciple now has a few small doubts, and begs the Teacher, in great compassion, to set them forth. The Master said: If you have a doubt, ask, and I shall speak it for you.

[Great assembly-feast] Also called the unrestrained assembly, in which, from the Buddhas and bodhisattvas above down to the hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals below, and likewise to people in this world, without distinction of wise and foolish, sage and ordinary, high and low, religious and lay, all are equally offered gifts of wealth and gifts of Dharma. [Scholars and commoners (shi-su)] Scholars (the lettered) and commoners (the ordinary). Shi-su also generally denotes the people, the common multitude, or the community without office. [Reverend (he-shang)] This is a Sanskrit term meaning “my teacher”; it is the respectful title that a monastic uses toward his own personal preceptor. [Inconceivable] Either the profound subtlety of principle, or the marvellous rarity of events, cannot be grasped by thought nor expressed in words.

Lord Wei said: Is that which the Reverend speaks not the essential aim of the Grand Master Bodhidharma? The Master said: It is. Lord Wei said: Your disciple has heard that when Bodhidharma first converted Emperor Wu of Liang, the Emperor asked: “In this life I have built monasteries, ordained monks, given alms, and made offerings—what merit is there?” Bodhidharma said: “There is no merit at all.” Your disciple has not grasped this principle, and begs the Reverend to explain it.]

Prefect Wei said: Is that which the Reverend has disclosed not the essential aim of the Grand Master Bodhidharma? The Master said: It is. Prefect Wei said: Your disciple has heard that when the Grand Master Bodhidharma first converted Emperor Wu of Liang, the Emperor asked: “In this life I have built monasteries, ordained monks, given alms, and made offerings—how much merit is there?” The Grand Master Bodhidharma answered: “There is not a single bit of merit.” Your disciple does not understand this principle, and begs the Teacher to explain it for me.

[Emperor Wu of Liang] The first emperor of the Liang, the southern dynasty. In the third year of the Tian-jian era (504 CE) he issued an edict declaring Buddhism the state religion; thereafter he gave himself four times into monasteries as a servant, and constantly held the unrestrained assembly, the great equanimity assembly, and the Ullambana assembly, and widely built monasteries and stupas. In the capital Jian-kang (today’s Nanjing) alone there were more than five hundred Buddhist monasteries and over a hundred thousand monks and nuns—this was the most flourishing era of Southern-dynasty Buddhism. [Zhen] The emperor’s style of self-designation. [There is no merit at all] The Grand Master Bodhidharma, in the eighth year of the Putong era of Liang (527 CE), crossed the sea and arrived in Nan-hai (today’s Guangzhou, Guangdong). The governor of Guangzhou received him with full ceremony; Emperor Wu sent a messenger to invite him to Jin-ling (today’s Nanjing, Jiangsu). Emperor Wu was a devoutly believing sovereign who, after taking the throne, built monasteries, copied sutras, ordained monks, and made images in great number, and so asked the Grand Master with self-satisfaction: “I have done so many Buddhist works—how much merit is there?” The Grand Master Bodhidharma said: “There is no merit at all.” The Emperor asked again: “Why is there no merit?” The Grand Master said: “These are conditioned activities, not true merit.” The Emperor did not comprehend; whereupon Bodhidharma crossed the river and entered Wei.

[The Master said: There is indeed no merit at all! Doubt not the words of the earlier sages. The Emperor’s mind was deviant, and he did not know the true Dharma. Building monasteries and ordaining monks, giving alms and making offerings—these are called seeking blessings; you must not take the blessings to be merit. Merit lies in the dharmakaya, not in cultivating blessings.]

The Master said: Though Emperor Wu built monasteries, ordained monks, gave alms, and made offerings in great number, there is indeed not a single bit of merit! Doubt not the words of the earlier sages, thinking the Grand Master Bodhidharma was mistaken. The Emperor harbored a deviant mind and did not know the true Dharma. Building monasteries and ordaining monks, giving alms and making offerings—this is cultivating blessings; you must not take these blessings as merit. Merit lies in one’s self-nature, and does not lie in cultivating blessings.

[Merit] To wipe out the inner ignorance is the meritorious work; for wisdom to come forth is the virtue. [Blessings (fude)] This refers to the meritorious bliss reaped from cultivating the good deeds of humans and heavenly beings. Blessings and merit are different: to cultivate the conditioned good that has outflows is blessings; only to realize within the Buddha-nature the wisdom that has no outflows is merit. Moreover, in cultivation, to cultivate while clinging to marks is blessings; to cultivate free of marks is merit. Emperor Wu cultivated good while clinging to marks, and so had only blessings and no merit. [Outflow (lou)] Another name for afflictions, carrying the two meanings of “leaking out” and “falling down.” The afflictions of greed, hatred, and ignorance, day and night, leak and flow out through the gates of the six sense-organs without ceasing, and so are called outflows. Also, afflictions cause one to fall down into the three evil destinies, and so are also called outflows. All dharmas that have afflictions are called “dharmas with outflows”; dharmas without afflictions are called “dharmas without outflows.” [Dharmakaya] This is the body of self-nature, the true body of the Buddha.

[The Master again said: Seeing nature is the meritorious work; evenness is the virtue. In thought after thought without obstruction, always seeing the true, marvellous function of one’s original nature, this is called merit. Inward humility is the meritorious work; outward practice of propriety is the virtue. Self-nature establishing the myriad dharmas is the meritorious work; the mind-essence free from thought is the virtue. Not departing from self-nature is the meritorious work; in application without defilement is the virtue. If you seek the merit-dharmakaya, but act according to this, that is true merit.]

The Master again said: Seeing nature is the meritorious work; the mind’s evenness is the virtue. In thought after thought, without pollution and without attachment, always seeing the true, marvellous function of one’s original nature, this is called merit. Inward humility is the meritorious work; outward practice of propriety is the virtue. Self-nature, taking the lead, establishing the myriad dharmas is the meritorious work; the mind-essence free from thought is the virtue. Not departing from self-nature is the meritorious work; in application without defilement is the virtue. If you would seek the merit-dharmakaya, merely practice according to this—that is true merit.

[Evenness] With no difference of high and low, noble and mean, deep and shallow—this is called evenness. The Records of the Five Lamps says: “Heaven is even, and so constantly covers; earth is even, and so constantly bears; sun and moon are even, and so the four seasons are constantly bright; nirvana is even, and so sage and ordinary are not two; the human mind is even, and so high and low have no contention.” [Propriety (li)] The norms of conduct that accord with the overall interest of the community. [Self-nature establishing the myriad dharmas is the meritorious work] This is self-nature, taking the lead, establishing the myriad dharmas—that is, as Chapter Four states: “The true-suchness self-nature gives rise to thought; though the six sense-organs have seeing, hearing, and knowing, they are not defiled by the myriad realms, and the true nature is always free.” [Merit-dharmakaya] The Tathagata, taking the merits of the myriad practices as the cause, accomplishes the fruit of the dharmakaya; hence it is called the merit-dharmakaya.

[One who cultivates merit, his mind does not disparage, and he constantly practices universal respect. If the mind constantly disparages people, and self and pride are not cut off, then naturally there is no meritorious work; if self-nature is false and unreal, then naturally there is no virtue. Because of self-glorifying greatness, one constantly disparages all things.]

One who would cultivate merit should have a mind that does not disparage, and constantly practice universal respect. If the mind constantly disparages others, always taking the self as the very center, with self, self, self unbroken—then naturally there is no meritorious work; if self-nature is false and unreal, then naturally there is no virtue. This is because, proud and self-glorifying, one constantly disparages all.

[Good-knowing friends! In thought after thought without break is the meritorious work; the mind’s conduct even and upright is the virtue. Cultivating one’s own nature is the meritorious work; cultivating one’s own body is the virtue.]

Good-knowing friends! In thought after thought, seeing nature without break, is the meritorious work; the mind’s conduct even and upright is the virtue. Cultivating one’s own mind-nature is the meritorious work; cultivating one’s own body-conduct is the virtue.

[Good-knowing friends! Merit must be seen within one’s self-nature, and is not what gift-giving and offerings seek, therefore blessings and merit differ. The Emperor did not know the true principle—it is not that our patriarch had any fault.]

Good-knowing friends! Merit must be seen within one’s own self-nature, and is not attained by outward gift-giving and offerings; therefore blessings and merit are different. Emperor Wu did not know the true principle of how merit is made, and so though his good deeds were many, in truth he had no merit—it is not that our patriarch spoke wrongly.

Q. When Bodhidharma first met Emperor Wu of Liang, the Emperor asked: “What is the highest meaning of the holy truths?” Bodhidharma said: “Vast and empty, there is no holy.” Then the Emperor went on to ask: “Who is it that confronts me?” Bodhidharma said: “I do not know.” The Emperor did not fall in with it, and so Bodhidharma crossed the river and went to the Wei. How should this exchange be understood?
